title: Never Play F6! | Master Class | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The Danish Gambit — d4 and e4, offering pawns to blast the position open for lightning-fast development.

A warning the whole title is built on — never play ...f6 in these open positions. The Damiano refutation runs on it: after ...f6 White has a queen check on h5, and the pawn stuck on e5 gets forked by the queen, hitting king and rook at once — a sacrifice as old as the 17th century.
We offer the second pawn with c3, and Black grabs it.
The bishop swings to c4, raking straight at f7.
And the second Danish bishop lands on b2 — now both bishops cut clear across the board at Black's king, the whole point of the double pawn sacrifice.
Black's bishop check on b4 is the computer's best try, though the theory runs deep and Black must be very accurate to hold — which shouldn't stop you playing the gambit at all.

Play with gambit mentality — once you've committed to a gambit, be ready to give up more than the initial pawn. Snatching material back with a move like Qxd4 the moment your e-pawn is hit would be inconsistent with the whole idea.
teaches: gambit mentality: consistency over grabbing back

moves.spoken: The classical antidote for Black, recommended for over a century, is d5 — giving one pawn straight back to open lines and speed his own development.
